extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and creative-writing students (especially those working in or across genres)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing genre fiction: identifying common genre conventions, honoring reader expectations, and techniques for thoughtful trope subversion and genre blending. Useful for authors aiming to work within or across mystery, thriller, sci‑fi, fantasy, romance, horror, YA, and mixed-genre fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — What tropes are
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring motifs, themes, conventional devices used in storytelling. Building blocks readers recognize and (often) crave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tropes are the familiar elements readers recognize; treat them as building blocks rather than cheating devices. Understanding what a trope is helps you decide whether to use it, honor it, or subvert it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meets reader expectations / reader trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader expectations — readers come to a genre with known expectations that affect satisfaction and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conventions to earn reader trust through competent execution. Failing to meet key expectations can break the contract between author and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing and discoverability
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing/discoverability — genre conventions help position work for the right audience and aid discoverability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow enough recognizable genre signals (cover, blurb, beats) so the book reaches its intended readers; mismatch between content and marketing can alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inherited craft wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherited craft wisdom — conventions encode hard-won craft lessons within a genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn conventions as distilled craft wisdom; they exist because they work for certain kinds of stories and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared cultural vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared cultural vocabulary — tropes give authors and readers a shorthand to communicate genre expectations and emotional payoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage shared motifs to create resonance, but be mindful of cultural meanings and sensitivities attached to certain tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality benchmark within a genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality benchmark within a genre — conventions set a baseline for assessing whether a work is competent for that genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genre-aware rubric should encode genre-specific quality criteria (not just generic 'literary' criteria) so reviewers and readers can judge fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery/Detective conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of crime/body at start; investigation (evidence, suspects, witnesses); red herrings; solution at the end; fair‑play clueing (golden‑age) or psychological focus (modern); the detective figure (amateur, professional, unconventional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to follow golden‑age fair play (clues visible to reader) or a modern psychological mystery. Ensure the investigation arc, clues, and resolution satisfy the genre's contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thriller conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two storylines: 'Stop!' (prevent catastrophe) or 'Run!' (flee); time pressure; escalating stakes; antagonist threat present from early; hero with specific skill set; action sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain tempo and palpable stakes; keep the antagonist threat visible and ensure action scenes advance plot and character rather than being gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fiction conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative premise extrapolated rigorously; 'What if' question driving the plot; sense of wonder; ideas as content; worldbuilding (technology, society, ecology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor speculative elements in logical extrapolation and show consequences; let the central idea meaningfully shape character and plot rather than being mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero's Journey common; magic system with internal rules; worldbuilding (history, geography, peoples); quest narrative often; good/evil moral architecture (often inverted in modern work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define consistent internal rules for magic or fantastical elements and use worldbuilding to create stakes and constraints; avoid flimsy deus ex machina resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance (RWA) conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Central love story; HEA (happily ever after) or HFN (happy for now) ending; meet‑cute / antagonism / dark moment / declaration; heat level appropriate to subgenre; two protagonists with mutual transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver the emotional arc and payoff readers expect for the subgenre (e.g., HEA/HFN); ensure the central relationship drives narrative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dread building; the threat (monster, ghost, idea, illness); vulnerable protagonist; moments of sudden intensity; often ambiguous resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain atmosphere and escalation of dread; use vulnerability and the unknown to generate fear; ambiguous endings are common but should still feel earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young Adult (YA) conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Teen protagonist + voice; coming‑of‑age themes; internal + external integrated; hopeful ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authentic teen voice and growth; integrate internal development with plot events and aim for an ending that offers hope or possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knows its conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Knows its conventions — reader trust earned by competent execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should demonstrate awareness and competence with a genre's core beats before attempting radical departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honors what readers come for
rubrics_metrics.description: Honors what readers come for — never breaks the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers expect certain payoffs (mystery's solution, romance's HEA), upend them only with clear and intentional reason; don't bait‑and‑switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subverts thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Subverts thoughtfully — when subverting, knows what's being subverted and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective subversion requires intimate knowledge of the trope and a clear narrative purpose; subversion should add meaning or insight, not just novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moves beyond cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: Moves beyond cliché — uses convention as scaffold, not crutch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar structures to support originality; avoid relying on tired motifs or stock characters without fresh specificity or stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity within convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity within convention — fresh rendering of familiar pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific in details, voice, and stakes so that conventional plots feel unique and lived‑in rather than generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intimately familiar with the trope first
rubrics_metrics.description: Be intimately familiar with the trope first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how the trope commonly functions (examples, history, reader expectations) before attempting to invert or subvert it; ignorance leads to hollow or confusing subversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversion techniques (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subversions: gender‑swap, role‑reversal, expectation‑flip. Examples given: 'Princess in distress who saves herself'; 'Villain as protagonist'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific techniques (gender‑swap, role reversal, point‑of‑view shift) and test whether the swap changes theme, stakes, or character agency in a meaningful way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversion must serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The subversion must serve the story, not just demonstrate cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid subversion for its own sake. Ask how the change deepens theme, character, or emotional payoff; if it doesn't, it may feel gimmicky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre blending as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Many great works combine genres (e.g., sci‑fi + thriller: Jurassic Park; fantasy + romance: Outlander; mystery + literary: The Secret History; horror + literary: Beloved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blending genres can create powerful hybrids, but the author should respect the conventions of each component genre and balance their expectations so readers aren't alienated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: slavishly following tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavishly following tropes (formulaic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overreliance on tropes leads to formulaic work; use conventions as scaffolding, then add specificity and risk to avoid predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: subverting without understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Subverting without understanding (broken expectation, unfulfilled promise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subversion that ignores the trope's function can leave readers feeling cheated because the narrative promise is unfulfilled; ensure subversions resolve or reframe expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: genre‑mismatched marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre‑mismatched marketing (alienates intended readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align cover, blurb, and metadata with the book's true genre mix; mislabeling harms discoverability and reader satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: genre snobbery
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre snobbery — refusing to learn from popular conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing popular conventions out of hand. Learning from effective genre techniques can improve craft even if your goal is literary innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication for quality models / rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'genre' rubric must encode genre‑specific quality criteria, not just 'literary' ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating evaluation models or reviewer guidelines, include genre‑aware dimensions (beats, payoffs, worldbuilding rules, heat levels, etc.) because reader expectations and success markers differ by genre.
